title: Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models ##### 94% on the benchmark, 31% on real invoices A logistics team in Chennai fine-tuned a vision-language model to extract data from delivery challans. They used a public document-VQA dataset for training, hit 94% field accuracy on its test split, and deployed to the warehouse. Real accuracy was 31%. The benchmark images were clean scans at 300 DPI, cropped to the document, correctly oriented. Their warehouse images were phone photographs taken in poor light, at an angle, often with a thumb in frame, sometimes rotated 90°, and roughly 40% contained handwritten annotations the printed-document dataset never showed. The model had learned to read clean scans. It had never learned to read a photograph of a crumpled challan on a loading dock. They retrained on 800 real warehouse images they labelled themselves. Benchmark accuracy dropped to 88%. **Real accuracy went to 91%.** **For VLMs, the gap between benchmark data and deployment data is usually larger than for text models**, because visual distribution shift is more severe and less obvious. Day 39 of the beginner track introduced VLMs; today is fine-tuning them properly. ##### VLM architecture The modular structure is what makes fine-tuning tractable. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Image
336×336"] --> B["Vision encoder
CLIP ViT-L/14
FROZEN usually"] B --> C["Patch embeddings
576 × 1024"] C --> D["Projector
MLP or resampler
TRAIN THIS"] D --> E["Image tokens
576 × 4096"] F["Text prompt"] --> G["Tokenizer"] G --> H["Text embeddings"] E --> I["LLM
Llama / Vicuna / Qwen
LoRA fine-tune"] H --> I I --> J["Generated text"] ``` **Three components, three different training strategies:** | Component | Parameters | Typical treatment | Why | |---|---|---|---| | Vision encoder | 300M–1B | **Frozen** | Already excellent at visual features | | Projector | 20–200M | **Fully trained** | Maps vision space → LLM token space | | LLM | 7B–70B | **LoRA** | Learns the task, preserves language ability | **The projector is the whole trick.** LLaVA's contribution was showing that a two-layer MLP mapping CLIP patch embeddings into the LLM's token embedding space is sufficient — the LLM then treats image patches as if they were tokens. You do not need to retrain either large component. ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class MLPProjector(nn.Module): """LLaVA-1.5 style: two-layer MLP, vision dim → LLM dim.""" def __init__(self, vision_dim=1024, llm_dim=4096, depth=2): super().__init__() layers = [nn.Linear(vision_dim, llm_dim)] for _ in range(depth - 1): layers += [nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(llm_dim, llm_dim)] self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers) def forward(self, image_features): # (B, n_patches, vision_dim) → (B, n_patches, llm_dim) return self.net(image_features) class PerceiverResampler(nn.Module): """Compress many patches to a fixed number of learned queries. Used by Qwen-VL and Flamingo. Fixes the token-count problem: 576 patches per image is expensive at high resolution or with multiple images. """ def __init__(self, vision_dim=1024, llm_dim=4096, n_queries=64, n_heads=16): super().__init__() self.queries = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_queries, llm_dim) * 0.02) self.kv_proj = nn.Linear(vision_dim, llm_dim) self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(llm_dim, n_heads, batch_first=True) self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(llm_dim) def forward(self, image_features): B = image_features.shape[0] kv = self.kv_proj(image_features) q = self.queries.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1) out, _ = self.attn(q, kv, kv) return self.norm(out + q) # (B, n_queries, llm_dim) ``` **Token count is the practical constraint.** A 336×336 image at patch size 14 gives 576 tokens. Four images in a conversation is 2,304 tokens before any text — and high-resolution processing (LLaVA-NeXT tiles the image) multiplies that by 4–5. A resampler compressing to 64 queries per image is what makes multi-image and long conversations affordable. ##### Image-text alignment Two-stage training, and the staging matters. **Stage 1 — projector pretraining.** Freeze both the vision encoder and the LLM; train only the projector on image-caption pairs. The projector learns to speak the LLM's embedding language. **Stage 2 — visual instruction tuning.** Unfreeze the LLM (via LoRA) and train on instruction-following data with images. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class VLMTrainingStage: name: str train_vision_encoder: bool train_projector: bool train_llm: str # "frozen" | "lora" | "full" learning_rate: float data_type: str epochs: int STAGES = [ VLMTrainingStage( name="projector_pretrain", train_vision_encoder=False, train_projector=True, train_llm="frozen", learning_rate=1e-3, # high — the projector starts random data_type="image-caption pairs (500k+)", epochs=1, ), VLMTrainingStage( name="visual_instruction_tune", train_vision_encoder=False, train_projector=True, train_llm="lora", learning_rate=2e-5, # low — LLM is pretrained data_type="visual instruction conversations (50k-500k)", epochs=1, ), VLMTrainingStage( name="domain_adaptation", # what you will actually do train_vision_encoder=False, train_projector=True, train_llm="lora", learning_rate=1e-4, data_type="your domain data (500-10k)", epochs=3, ), ] ``` **You will almost always start from an already-aligned model** — LLaVA-1.6, Qwen2-VL, InternVL — and run only the third stage. Stage 1 requires 500,000+ caption pairs and is not something a product team does. **Different learning rates per component** is essential. The projector wants 1e-3 in stage 1 and around 1e-4 later; the LLM LoRA wants 1e-4 to 2e-4 (Day 12's guidance). One learning rate for both either fails to train the projector or destroys the LLM. ##### Building the dataset The Chennai lesson. Your data must match deployment conditions. ```python import json from pathlib import Path from typing import Literal def build_vlm_example(image_path: str, conversations: list[dict], metadata: dict = None) -> dict: """LLaVA-format training example.""" return { "id": Path(image_path).stem, "image": image_path, "conversations": conversations, "metadata": metadata or {}, } EXAMPLE = build_vlm_example( image_path="warehouse/challan_8821.jpg", conversations=[ {"from": "human", "value": "\nExtract the challan details as JSON " "with fields: challan_no, date (YYYY-MM-DD), " "consignor, consignee, packages, weight_kg. " "Use null for fields not legible."}, {"from": "gpt", "value": json.dumps({ "challan_no": "CH-2026-04471", "date": "2026-03-14", "consignor": "Bharat Textiles, Tiruppur", "consignee": "Metro Retail, Chennai", "packages": 18, "weight_kg": 214.5, }, indent=2)}, ], metadata={"source": "warehouse_camera", "quality": "poor_light", "has_handwriting": True, "rotation_deg": 0}, ) ``` **The `` token placement matters.** It marks where image tokens are spliced into the text sequence. Different models expect it in different positions — check the model's processor before assuming. **Dataset composition for a document-extraction task:** | Category | Share | Why | |---|---|---| | Clean, well-lit, straight | 25% | The easy baseline | | Poor lighting | 20% | Warehouse reality | | Angled or rotated | 15% | Phone photography | | Partially obscured | 10% | Thumbs, folds, staples | | Handwritten annotations | 15% | Common on real documents | | **Illegible fields** | **10%** | **Must output null, not guess** | | Wrong document type | 5% | Must refuse, not extract | **The last two categories are the most important and most often omitted.** A model that hallucinates a challan number when the field is smudged is worse than one that returns null — and Day 35's grounding discipline applies identically to vision. ```python ILLEGIBLE_EXAMPLE = build_vlm_example( image_path="warehouse/challan_9102.jpg", conversations=[ {"from": "human", "value": "\nExtract the challan details as JSON..."}, {"from": "gpt", "value": json.dumps({ "challan_no": "CH-2026-04502", "date": None, # date field is smudged "consignor": "Sri Lakshmi Traders", "consignee": None, # covered by a fold "packages": 6, "weight_kg": None, }, indent=2)}, ], metadata={"deliberately_illegible": ["date", "consignee", "weight_kg"]}, ) ``` **How much data?** For domain adaptation on a narrow task, 500–2,000 well-labelled examples is usually enough. Below 300 you will overfit; above 5,000 returns diminish sharply unless the task is genuinely diverse. ##### Fine-tuning with LoRA ```python import torch from transformers import (AutoProcessor, LlavaNextForConditionalGeneration, TrainingArguments, Trainer, BitsAndBytesConfig) from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training MODEL_ID = "llava-hf/llava-v1.6-mistral-7b-hf" bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig( load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = LlavaNextForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, quantization_config=bnb, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", ) model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model, use_gradient_checkpointing=True) lora_config = LoraConfig( r=32, lora_alpha=64, lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM", # Language model attention and MLP — NOT the vision tower target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], # Train the projector fully alongside the LoRA adapters modules_to_save=["multi_modal_projector"], ) model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable: ~91M of 7.6B (1.2%) — 40M LoRA + 51M projector ``` **`modules_to_save=["multi_modal_projector"]` is the critical line.** The projector must adapt to your visual domain, and LoRA on it is less effective than full training because it is small and its input distribution has shifted. Omitting this is the most common VLM fine-tuning mistake. **Never target the vision tower.** It is frozen for good reason — CLIP's visual features generalise well, and fine-tuning them on 800 images causes catastrophic forgetting of general visual understanding. **Rank 32 rather than 16.** Visual instruction tuning shifts the LLM's behaviour more than a text style adaptation does, and the extra capacity helps. Day 12's rank guidance applies, shifted up one notch. ##### The data collator The part that is fiddly and where bugs hide. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass from PIL import Image import torch IGNORE_INDEX = -100 @dataclass class VLMDataCollator: processor: any max_length: int = 2048 def __call__(self, examples: list[dict]) -> dict: images, texts, prompt_lengths = [], [], [] for ex in examples: image = Image.open(ex["image"]).convert("RGB") images.append(image) convs = ex["conversations"] messages = [] for turn in convs: role = "user" if turn["from"] == "human" else "assistant" messages.append({"role": role, "content": turn["value"]}) # Full text for input full = self.processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False) texts.append(full) # Prompt-only, to compute the mask boundary prompt_only = self.processor.apply_chat_template( messages[:-1], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) prompt_lengths.append( len(self.processor.tokenizer(prompt_only, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"])) batch = self.processor( text=texts, images=images, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=self.max_length, ) labels = batch["input_ids"].clone() labels[labels == self.processor.tokenizer.pad_token_id] = IGNORE_INDEX # Mask the prompt — Day 13's loss masking, applied here for i, plen in enumerate(prompt_lengths): labels[i, :plen] = IGNORE_INDEX # Mask image token positions — they have no text target image_token_id = self.processor.tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("") labels[batch["input_ids"] == image_token_id] = IGNORE_INDEX batch["labels"] = labels return batch ``` **Masking the image token positions is specific to VLMs** and easy to miss. Those positions hold image embeddings, not text, and computing a language-modelling loss over them is meaningless — it produces gradients that push the projector toward predicting text tokens from image patches, which degrades alignment. **Verify the masking by decoding**, exactly as Day 13 recommended: ```python def verify_vlm_masking(collator, examples, processor): batch = collator(examples[:1]) ids = batch["input_ids"][0] labels = batch["labels"][0] learned = ids[labels != IGNORE_INDEX] print("FULL SEQUENCE:", processor.tokenizer.decode(ids)[:500]) print("\nLEARNED FROM:", processor.tokenizer.decode(learned)[:500]) print(f"\nmasked {100 * (labels == IGNORE_INDEX).float().mean():.0f}% of positions") ``` If `LEARNED FROM` contains the prompt or `` placeholders, your masking is broken. ##### Training configuration ```python from transformers import TrainingArguments, Trainer args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./llava-challan", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=2, # images are memory-hungry gradient_accumulation_steps=8, learning_rate=1e-4, lr_scheduler_type="cosine", warmup_ratio=0.03, weight_decay=0.0, max_grad_norm=0.3, bf16=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, gradient_checkpointing_kwargs={"use_reentrant": False}, optim="paged_adamw_8bit", dataloader_num_workers=4, remove_unused_columns=False, # ← REQUIRED for VLM datasets eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=50, save_strategy="steps", save_steps=50, load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="eval_loss", logging_steps=10, seed=42, ) trainer = Trainer( model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_dataset, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, data_collator=VLMDataCollator(processor), ) trainer.train() ``` **`remove_unused_columns=False` is mandatory.** The Trainer's default behaviour strips columns not matching the model's forward signature, which deletes the `image` field and produces a confusing error about missing pixel values. **Batch size 1–2 with heavy accumulation.** A single 336×336 image at high resolution can consume 2–3 GB of activations. Gradient checkpointing is not optional. **Separate learning rates** if you want the projector trained faster than the LoRA adapters: ```python optimizer_grouped_parameters = [ {"params": [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "multi_modal_projector" in n and p.requires_grad], "lr": 2e-4}, {"params": [p for n, p in model.named_parameters() if "lora" in n and p.requires_grad], "lr": 1e-4}, ] optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(optimizer_grouped_parameters, weight_decay=0.0) trainer = Trainer(..., optimizers=(optimizer, None)) ``` ##### Image preprocessing Where a lot of real-world accuracy lives, and where the Chennai team's second fix came from. ```python from PIL import Image, ImageOps, ImageEnhance import numpy as np def preprocess_document_image(path: str, target_size=672, auto_orient=True, enhance=True) -> Image.Image: """Normalise phone photos of documents before the model sees them.""" img = Image.open(path) # 1. Respect EXIF orientation — phones rotate via metadata, not pixels img = ImageOps.exif_transpose(img) img = img.convert("RGB") # 2. Detect and correct 90/180/270 rotation if auto_orient: img = _correct_orientation(img) # 3. Enhance legibility for poor-light captures if enhance: img = ImageEnhance.Contrast(img).enhance(1.3) img = ImageEnhance.Sharpness(img).enhance(1.2) # 4. Resize preserving aspect ratio, pad to square img.thumbnail((target_size, target_size), Image.LANCZOS) padded = Image.new("RGB", (target_size, target_size), (255, 255, 255)) padded.paste(img, ((target_size - img.width) // 2, (target_size - img.height) // 2)) return padded def _correct_orientation(img: Image.Image) -> Image.Image: """Use text-line orientation to detect rotation. Cheap heuristic.""" import cv2 gray = cv2.cvtColor(np.array(img), cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY) edges = cv2.Canny(gray, 50, 150) lines = cv2.HoughLines(edges, 1, np.pi / 180, threshold=200) if lines is None: return img angles = [np.degrees(theta) % 180 for (_, theta) in lines[:50, 0]] dominant = float(np.median(angles)) if 80 < dominant < 100: # text lines are vertical return img.rotate(90, expand=True) return img ``` **`ImageOps.exif_transpose` alone fixes a surprising fraction of failures.** Phone cameras store orientation in EXIF metadata rather than rotating the pixels; a naive `Image.open` gives you a sideways document, and the model has no idea what it is looking at. **Apply the same preprocessing at training and inference.** A model trained on enhanced images and served raw ones sees a distribution it never learned — the same principle as tokenizer consistency from Day 4. ##### Evaluating VLMs Text metrics are insufficient. Evaluate on the task. ```python import json from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable, Optional @dataclass class VLMEvalCase: image_path: str prompt: str expected: dict category: str # "clean" | "poor_light" | "illegible" | ... illegible_fields: set = None def evaluate_extraction(model, processor, cases: list[VLMEvalCase]) -> dict: """Field-level accuracy, plus the crucial null-handling check.""" from collections import defaultdict field_correct = defaultdict(int) field_total = defaultdict(int) by_category = defaultdict(lambda: {"correct": 0, "total": 0}) hallucinated_nulls = 0 null_opportunities = 0 parse_failures = 0 for case in cases: image = preprocess_document_image(case.image_path) output = generate_vlm(model, processor, image, case.prompt, max_new_tokens=400, temperature=0.0) try: predicted = json.loads(_extract_json(output)) except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError): parse_failures += 1 by_category[case.category]["total"] += 1 continue all_fields_ok = True for field, expected_value in case.expected.items(): field_total[field] += 1 got = predicted.get(field) if _values_match(got, expected_value): field_correct[field] += 1 else: all_fields_ok = False # The check that matters: did it invent a value for an illegible field? if expected_value is None: null_opportunities += 1 if got is not None: hallucinated_nulls += 1 by_category[case.category]["total"] += 1 by_category[case.category]["correct"] += int(all_fields_ok) return { "field_accuracy": {f: round(field_correct[f] / field_total[f], 3) for f in field_total}, "overall_field_accuracy": round( sum(field_correct.values()) / max(sum(field_total.values()), 1), 3), "exact_match_by_category": { c: round(v["correct"] / max(v["total"], 1), 3) for c, v in by_category.items()}, "hallucination_rate_on_illegible": round( hallucinated_nulls / max(null_opportunities, 1), 3), "json_parse_failure_rate": round(parse_failures / len(cases), 3), } ``` **`hallucination_rate_on_illegible` is the metric that separates a usable extractor from a dangerous one.** A model with 91% field accuracy that invents plausible values for smudged fields will silently corrupt your data; one at 88% that returns null is trustworthy. **Report by category.** Overall accuracy hides that poor-light images are at 62% while clean scans are at 97% — and that breakdown is what tells you which data to collect more of. **Public benchmarks worth knowing:** DocVQA and InfographicVQA for documents, ChartQA for charts, TextVQA for scene text, MMMU for general multimodal reasoning, and MathVista for visual maths. Use them to sanity-check general capability has not regressed — the Day 11 forgetting concern applies to VLMs too. ##### Serving ```python from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams from PIL import Image llm = LLM( model="./llava-challan-merged", trust_remote_code=True, max_model_len=4096, limit_mm_per_prompt={"image": 2}, # cap images per request gpu_memory_utilization=0.90, ) params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=400) outputs = llm.generate({ "prompt": "USER: \nExtract the challan details as JSON.\nASSISTANT:", "multi_modal_data": {"image": Image.open("challan.jpg")}, }, params) ``` **`limit_mm_per_prompt` matters for capacity planning.** Each image is 576–2,880 tokens depending on resolution handling, and an unbounded image count lets one request consume your entire KV cache budget. **Cost implications:** a high-resolution image on a hosted API costs 1,000–2,000 tokens. At 40,000 documents a day that is 40–80 million tokens of input, which is exactly the arithmetic that pushes teams toward a fine-tuned small VLM on their own hardware. ##### Common mistakes - **Training on benchmark data that does not match deployment conditions** — 94% to 31%. - **Omitting `modules_to_save=["multi_modal_projector"]`**, leaving the projector unadapted. - **Fine-tuning the vision encoder** on a small dataset. - **Not masking image token positions** in the labels. - **`remove_unused_columns=True`**, which strips the image column. - **Ignoring EXIF orientation** — sideways documents the model cannot read. - **Different preprocessing at training and inference.** - **No illegible-field examples**, so the model hallucinates rather than returning null. - **Evaluating with text metrics** instead of field-level task accuracy. - **One learning rate** for the projector and the LoRA adapters. - **Unbounded images per request**, blowing the KV cache budget. - **Not checking general capability regression** after domain fine-tuning. ##### Hands-on: collect real data first Your practical task fine-tunes a small VLM with LoRA on a visual instruction dataset. Before writing any training code, collect 50 images from your actual deployment conditions and run the base model on them — that baseline tells you whether fine-tuning is needed and, more usefully, which failure categories dominate. Then build your training set to match that distribution. The mini project builds a document-understanding assistant extracting structured data from images. **Include 10% illegible-field examples** where the correct answer is null, and measure `hallucination_rate_on_illegible` explicitly. Combine with Day 18's constrained decoding so the output is guaranteed-valid JSON — the two techniques compose well, and together they produce an extractor you can actually trust in a pipeline. The assignment explains VLM architecture and plans a fine-tune for a chosen visual domain. Cover the three components and why each gets different treatment, the two-stage training rationale, and then the concrete plan: how many images, what distribution of conditions, what you will label, what you will measure, and what your null-handling strategy is. The data plan is the part that determines success, so give it the most space. ##### Key takeaways - **VLMs are three components with three training strategies** — frozen vision encoder, fully-trained projector, LoRA on the LLM — and `modules_to_save` on the projector is the line people forget. - **Deployment distribution matters more than benchmark scores.** Phone photos in poor light at an angle are a different visual domain from clean 300 DPI scans. - **Mask image token positions in the labels**, set `remove_unused_columns=False`, and verify masking by decoding what the model learns from. - **Include illegible-field examples where the answer is null**, and measure hallucination on them — a model that invents smudged values is worse than a less accurate one that abstains. - **Normalise images identically at training and inference**, starting with EXIF orientation, which alone fixes a meaningful fraction of real-world failures.
practical_task_reference: Fine-tune a small VLM with LoRA on a visual-instruction dataset for a specific image-understanding task.
mini_project_reference: Build a document-understanding assistant by fine-tuning a VLM to extract structured data from images.
assignment_reference: Write an explainer of VLM architecture and a plan for fine-tuning one on a chosen visual domain.
